stem: A32-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. He has suffered from increasing headaches over the past ten weeks,typically at night, occurring 1-2 hours after he goes to sleep. The headache always comes on the left-hand side of his head and typically lasts between 45 and 90 minutes. He has tearing, conjunctival injection and facial flushing at the time of the attacks. Attacks occur, on average, three times per day. Neurological examination in the clinic is normal. Which of the following is likely to be most useful in controlling his headache over the long term?
explanation: Verapamil is the intervention of choice for prophylaxis in cluster headache. It is started at a dose of 40 mg twice daily and can be slowly increased up to a total dose of 960 mg/day. Where doses increase above 120 mg daily, then monitoring of electrocardiograms is recommended at least every two weeks, corresponding with a dose increase. Both constipation and skin flushing may limit uptitration of the dose, and it is contraindicated in patients with significant heart failure and left ventricular dysfunction. Q.

stem: A32-year-old woman who has systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), currently managed with azathioprine, is 16 weeks pregnant with her first child. She is concerned about the risks of her child developing neonatal complete heart block. Which of the following antibodies is most at risk of causing neonatal heart block?
explanation: Anti-Ro antibodies target two Ro proteins(Ro 52 and Ro 60). The significance in maternal lupus is that they can result in neonatal heart block where symptoms of bradycardia persist for up to six months. Immunosuppression in the mother reduces the risk of neonatal heart block occurring, and in some cases, intravenous(IV) immunoglobulin has been used to successfully prevent it. Q.

stem: A 47-year-old man comes to the Ophthalmology Clinic for review. He has noticed visual field loss, being more marked on the left than on the right, where he loses sight of objects at his feet. Mapping of his visual fields at the optometrist has demonstrated near-complete loss of the lower half of the visual field on the left-hand side and loss of two-thirds of the lower half of the visual field on the right-hand side. Which of the following is the most likely location of any lesion causing the visual field loss?
explanation: Craniopharyngioma leads predominantly to superior pressure on the optic chiasm. This leads to progressive inferior visual field loss with an inferior heminopsia, as seen here. Tumour growth may be more marked on one side than on the other, accounting for greater visual field loss on the left than on the right in this case. Magnetic resonance imaging(MRI) is the investigation of choice. Q.

stem: A41-year-old woman who has Graves' disease treated with a block-and-replace regimen comes to the Emergency Department with worsening vision. On examination, she has marked proptosis, with lid lag and conjunctival injection, consistent with Graves'ophthalmopathy. She complains of blurred vision and loss of colour vision, particularly over the last 24 hours, and her visual acuity has deteriorated markedly since her clinic visit one month earlier. She is prescribed high-dose corticosteroids. Which of the following additional interventions is the most appropriate?
explanation: Toclizumab is an anti-interleukin 6 monoclonal antibody. In a randomised controlled trial, treatment with tocilizumab was associated with a greater improvement in clinical activity score at 16 weeks, compared with placebo (93.3% versus 58.8%, respectively), and an improvement in composite ophthalmic score at 16 weeks, compared to placebo(73.3% versus 29.4%,respectively). Further studies have demonstrated a positive impact in steroid-resistant Graves' disease. Q.

stem: A32-year-old man is reviewed in the Cancer Genetics Clinic following a diagnosis of Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer). His brother died from colorectal cancer aged 39,and his father passed away from colon cancer at the age of 48.The patient has had two right-sided colonic adenomas(1.2 cm and 1.4 cm) resected at colonoscopy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Aspirin 600 mg has been proven in clinical studies to reduce the risk of colorectal cancer in patients with Lynch syndrome when given for more than two years. A total of 861 patients received aspirin or placebo for a period of 2-4 years. A significant reduction in colon cancer risk was seen (hazard ratio 0.41, confidence interval 0.19-0.86), which persisted for up to ten years. A reduction in non-colon cancer was detected, although this did not reach statistical significance.

stem: A 29-year-old nurse is reviewed in the Emergency Department following a needlestick injury from an intravenous (IV) drug abuser who is known to be a hepatitis B carrier. The nurse has been vaccinated against hepatitis B and is known to have never been infected with the virus. Which of the following is the best way to assess her level of hepatitis B immunity?
explanation: Anti-HBs antibodies are used to assess the effectiveness of hepatitis B vaccination, which stimulates an antibody response to the surface antigen. Levels above 100 mlU/ml indicate a good level of immunity where no further action is required. Levels between 10 and 100 mlU/ml indicate the need for a booster vaccination, and levels below 10 mlU/ml indicate that the patient is a non-responder to vaccination and is unlikely to be immune. Q.

stem: A39-year-old woman comes to the Endocrine Clinic for review. She has lost 5kg in weight over the past two months; she has palpitations and has been increasingly anxious. Her blood pressure is 108/82 mmHg, and pulse 98 bpm and regular. She has a smooth goitre, which is mildly tender on palpation, and a fine tremor at rest. Her thyroid-stimulating hormone(TSH) is0.05 mlU/L. Which of the following is the primary cause of her thyrotoxicosis?
explanation: Stimulating TSH receptor antibodies are the primary cause of thyrotoxicosis in patients with Graves' disease. The antibodies are produced by B-cells, and this antibody production is thought to occur as a result of defective T-cell/B-cell crosstalk where the TSH receptor is singled out as an autoantigen. This leads to increased production of thyroid hormone, in contrast to destructive thyroiditis where there is increased release of stored thyroid hormone. Dificulty:Average Bc.

explanation: Duloxetine is a serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor used for the treatment of stress incontinence. It also has evidence to support its use in depression. stem: A 48-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department following a collapse at work. By the time she is admitted to the department, she has regained consciousness and has a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 15.She tells you she feels weak. The Triage Nurse does routine observations and hands you an electrocardiogram(ECG) for review. You note U waves are present on the ECG. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her U waves?
explanation: Hypokalaemia is well recognised as a cause of U waves.U waves consist of a small deflection immediately after the T wave, usually going in the same direction as the T wave. Other causes of U waves include: · hypocalcaemia · hypomagnesaemia · hypothermia · raised intracranial pressure ·left ventricular hypertrophy · hypertrophic cardiomyopathy · bradycardia · drugs, including digoxin, phenothiazines and class 1a and 3 anti-arrhythmics. In this case, the collapse is most likely to have been related to hypokalaemia. Potassium Imbalance Media explanations.

Her only other complaint is that she is unable to smell. Her blood pressure is 122/78 mmHg, and her pulse is 70 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 22 kg/m.You note that she has a long arm span,no axillary hair, sparse pubic hair and minimal breast development. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 136 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count(WCC) 7.5×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 240×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.2 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 99 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of her delayed puberty?
explanation: Hypogonadotrophic hypopituitarism is the likely diagnosis here, with the lack of sense of smell, a big pointer to Kallmann syndrome, with failure of development of the olfactory bulb. This leads to failure of gonadotrophin production, and failure therefore to enter puberty. It is possible to induce ovulation in women with the condition by giving pulsed gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) therapy. Hypopituitarism And Growth Hormone Deficiency In Adults explanations.

He has confusion and dysphasia. He has diabetes mellitus and hypertension, and smokes 20 cigarettes per day. According to his wife, the weakness began some two hours earlier. His blood pressure is 178/95 mmHg and his pulse is 95 bpm and regular. You confirm the presence of weakness consistent with an acute stroke. A range of trials have shown benefit with respect to outcomes, with between 40% and 60% improvement in patients achieving a good outcome post- stroke at six months. Between 4.5 and 6 hours, thrombolysis can still be considered, contingent upon further imaging to determine cerebral blood flow. Cerebrovascular Disease and Stroke Media explanations.

explanation: Stool frequency is the most important marker of UC severity, according to the Montreal classification. Four or less stools per day is generally considered to be a marker of mild disease;4 stools per day with minimal signs of systemic toxicity is generally considered moderate UC. At least six stools per day is seen as a marker of severe UC, especially when there are signs of systemic toxicity such as pyrexia, toxicity and raised inflammatory markers. It is endemic in areas of poor sanitation, although cases have been reported in the United Kingdom, albeit rare. Nitazoxanide can be used as an alternative to co-trimoxazole in patients who are unable to take sulfa-based compounds. Cryptosporidiosis Media explanations.

stem: A 65-year-old retired machinist comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. Her main complaint is of pain and stiffness affecting the distal interphalangeal (DIP)joints. On examination, you note marked bony swelling and stiffness over the DIP joints. There are no signs of nail pitting. What is the most likely cause of the changes affecting her fingers?
explanation: This patient's symptoms are consistent with Heberden's nodes, bony arthritic lesions affecting the DIP joints of the fingers, often as a result of chronic overuse. It is, for example, seen in patients who used an old- fashioned typewriter or in people who worked in the sewing industry. Pain-relieving medications and finger exercises are the mainstay of therapy.

stem: A 67-year-old man who uses intermittent peritoneal dialysis to manage his end-stage renal failure comes to the Emergency Department. He has been unable to completely drain out his overnight bag and it is cloudy. He also has abdominal pain. His temperature is 38.2°℃, blood pressure 115/83 mmHg and pulse 92 bpm and regular. His abdomen is mildly distended, with active bowel sounds; it is generally tender. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 93 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 16.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 301×10/L 150-400×10/ Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.8mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 542μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 225 mg/l 10 mg/l Peritoneal fluid microscopy 250 white cells per ml, no organisms Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This is the regimen of choice where either no organism is identified or a mixed growth of Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms is identified on microscopy. Vancomycin covers staphylococcal infection, and ciprofloxacin covers Gram-negative pathogens. Although ciprofloxacin is not routinely recommended, according to the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency(MHRA) guidance, this is one situation where it should still be considered. It is possible to develop recurrent episodes of peritonitis and to develop chronic bacterial carriage because of tube colonisation. Apart from the risks associated with sepsis, this can also cause fibrin bands and adhesions to develop within the peritoneum, reducing the efficiency of dialysis by the peritoneal route over time. Recurrent peritonitis is defined as another episode occurring within four weeks of cessation of antibiotics. Where this leads to decreased efficiency of dialysis, a change of dialysis catheter may be required. Patients should also have their dialysis technique observed to make sure no errors have crept in which would increase the risk of infection.

stem: A 62-year-old man who has suffered an ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is treated with a left anterior descending (LAD) stent and is now taking a combination of aspirin and ticagrelor. Which of the following fits best with the mode of action of ticagrelor?
explanation: P2Y12 inhibitor adenosine diphosphate (ADP)-mediated P2Y12-dependent platelet activation and aggregation. Ticagrelor does not prevent ADP binding, but when bound to the P2Y12 receptor, it prevents ADP-induced signal transduction. Since platelets participate in the initiation and/or evolution of thrombotic complications of atherosclerotic disease, inhibition of platelet function has been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events such as death, myocardial infarction or stroke.

stem: An 18-year-old woman who has Turner syndrome comes to the clinic for review with her mother. She is concerned about long-term complications of the disease,including osteoporosis. Which of the following is the optimal way to reduce her risk of osteoporosis?
explanation: This patient needs physiological levels of hormone replacement to protect against osteoporosis. Hormone replacement therapy is therefore the most appropriate intervention. Pubertal oestrogen replacement is normally commenced with low-dose transdermal oestrogen. Over time, the doseis increased and the patient eventually is moved to a combined oestrogen and progesterone pill.

explanation: This patient has microcytic anaemia, with abnormal liver function tests and liver metastases identified on the Liver ultrasound scan. Given the absence of upper or lower Gl symptoms, a right-sided colonic cancer is the potential cause of her presentation. The optimal next step is confirmation with a tissue diagnosis, so that therapy can be appropriately targeted. As such, colonoscopy is the most useful investigation given the diagnosis of colonic cancer.

stem: A 42-year-old woman comes to the Rheumatology Clinic with progressive weakness. She is finding it increasingly hard to get up out of a low chair, comb her hair and climb the stairs. She is not able to continue with her job as a guide at the local museum. She has no medical illnesses and takes no regular medication. Her blood pressure is 118/80 mmHg,and pulse 82 bpm and regular. You confirm 4/5 power weakness affecting the proximal muscles of her upper and lower limbs. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 110 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 10.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 339×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 98 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) 1.3 mlU/L 0.5-4.5 mlU/L Creatine kinase(CK) 1273 U/L 22-198 U/L Which of the following antibodies are most specific for the likely diagnosis here?
explanation: Anti-Jo 1 antibodies are found in around 20% of patients with polymyositis, the most likely diagnosis, given there is proximal myopathy and a marked elevation in CK.Distal muscles are spared, such that fine movements of the fingers remain entirely preserved. As the condition progresses, there is pharyngeal weakness and difficulty swallowing. Corticosteroids are the initial intervention of choice.

stem: A 45-year-old alcoholic is reviewed in the Emergency Department. He has severe epigastric pain and vomiting over the past 12 hours. As well as one previous admission with acute pancreatitis, he has duodenitis for which he takes omeprazole. His temperature is 38.1℃, blood pressure 95/82 mmHg and pulse 100 bpm and regular. He is thin and very tender in the epigastrium, with guarding. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 102 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 11.9×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 109×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.2 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 143 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Amylase 390 IU/L 30-220 IU/L Calcium 2.55 mmol/L 2.2-2.60 mmol/L Glucose 6.9 mmol/L 7 mmol/L Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 65 IU/L 10-40 IU/L Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 62 IU/L 5-35 IU/L Bilirubin 8 μmol/L 0-17μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Given the evidence of shock here with hypotension, tachycardia and pyrexia, as well as epigastric pain and guarding, a perforated duodenal ulcer is the most likely diagnosis, especially given the patient is known to have peptic ulcer disease. A modest increase in amylase fits with the diagnosis. Abdominal CT is the investigation of choice to confirm the diagnosis.

stem: A72-year-old woman is referred to the Dermatology Clinic with a painful, blistering skin rash, with multiple lesions over her body and affecting her mucous membranes. The blisters are flaccid and rupture to leave painful skin erosions. She tells you that the blisters appeared first in her mouth and then progressed rapidly. Examination reveals multiple flaccid blisters, skin erosions and extensive ulcers within the oral cavity. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 109 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 10.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 322×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 104 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 47 mg/l 10 mg/l Which of the following is the most likely cause of her skin changes?
explanation: Media explanations Pemphigus vulgaris, the most likely diagnosis here, begins in the majority of patients with flaccid blisters occurring first in the mouth and then rapidly spreading to involve the body. The blisters are large, flaccid and painful, but are not usually particularly itchy. It occurs because of antibodies to desmoglein 3(DSG3) and DSG1, which act as the glue holding keratinocytes together. For patients like this here with extensive disease, high-dose systemic corticosteroids are usually required to achieve remission.

stem: A52-year-old woman is recommended for a chemotherapy regimen which incorporates trastuzumab as part of her regimen. Which of the following is the most important adverse effect of trastuzumab therapy?
explanation: Agonism of the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2(HER2) receptor, which is the target of trastuzumab(Herceptin@), is thought to be protective against dilated cardiomyopathy. Antagonism of the receptor with trastuzumab has a significant impact on the risk of cardiomyopathy and cardiac failure. Co- prescription with taxane therapies and doxorubicin can worsen this risk further.

stem: A 29-year-old man presents to the clinic for review. He has suffered from increasing lethargy and intermittent diarrhoea over the past few months. He underwent a splenectomy some ten years ago and tells you his brother and father have also had their spleens removed. His blood film shows a number of red blood cells containing Howell-Jolly bodies(HJBs). Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis carries an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern in 75% of cases and fits with the pattern here of the patient, his brother and his father having undergone therapeutic splenectomy. A red cell membrane defect in both spectrin and ankyrin is seen, which leads to the cells taking a typical spherocyte shape and being susceptible to haemolysis. Over time, hypersplenism and an increased risk of gallstones are seen. Splenectomy significantly reduces haemolysis and the subsequent risk of gall bladder disease.

stem: A52-year-old woman who has systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) comes to the clinic for her routine appointment. Current medication includes hydroxychloroquine for control of lupus-related joint symptoms Over the past two months, she has felt increasingly tired. Her blood pressure is 149/89 mmHg, and her pulse is 74 bpm and regular. Her joint symptoms appear under control. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 108 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.7×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 332×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 145(up from 115 over past three months) 50-120 μmol/L Urine Protein ++, blood++ Which of the following is the most appropriate way to treat her lupus?
explanation: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Media explanations Mycophenolate mofetil and cyclophosphamide have broadly similar efficacy in achieving nephritis remission and are first-choice treatment options. Patient type may influence therapy choice, with an increased response to mycophenolate mofetil seen in patients of African and Hispanic origin, and cyclophosphamide is generally avoided in younger patients, particularly those of childbearing potential. The usual dosing regimen is 0.5g of mycophenolate mofetil twice daily for the first week, then 1g twice daily for the second week, and after this 1.5 g twice daily. Using a remission definition which includes both Cr and albuminuria levels, this regimen achieved remission in just over 50% of patients in the largest intervention study of 370 patients.

stem: A 34-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with shortness of breath and a productive cough with purulent sputum over the past 24 hours. He is usually well and takes no regular medications. His temperature is 38.9°℃, blood pressure 105/80 mmHg and pulse 95 bpm and regular. Oxygen saturation is 91% on air. There are signs of consolidation at the right base on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 143 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 17.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 372×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 102 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 231 mg/l 10 mg/l Chest X-ray (CXR) Right lower lobe consolidation Which of the following is the most likely cause of his low measured oxygen saturation?
options: Poor peripheral perfusion in his fingers
explanation: Pneumonia Media explanations Intrapulmonary shunting occurs early in pneumonia and is thought to be responsible for hypoxia occurring early in the disease. This is where blood flow is preferentially directed to consolidated areas of the lung where oxygen diffusion capacity is the poorest and blood flow is actually reduced to areas of the lung where gas exchange is much better.

stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the Cardiology Clinic for review. She has been referred by her General Practitioner (GP) with a murmur suspicious of tricuspid regurgitation and a provisional diagnosis of Ebstein's anomaly. Which of the following would you expect to find on cardiovascular evaluation?
options: Elevated jugular venous pressure(JVP) on physical examination
Left bundle branch block on electrocardiogram (ECG)
Right bundle branch block on ECG
explanation: Right bundle branch block in patients with Ebstein's anomaly may be complete or incomplete.P waves may be broad and tall; R waves are small in leads V1 and V2, and abnormalities of the terminal QRS pattern may also be seen. Patients with Ebstein's anomaly are susceptible to arrhythmia, particularly paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. Early surgery for Ebstein's anomaly is thought to reduce progression of right heart failure and improve overall survival. Patients presenting in adulthood are thought to have less severe abnormalities. Ebstein's anomaly is a malformation of the tricuspid valve and the right ventricle. It is characterised by: · adherence of the septal and posterior leaflets to the underlying myocardium · downward displacement of the functional annulus · dilation of the 'atrialised' portion of the right ventricle, with potential hypertrophy and thinning of the wall · redundancy,fenestrations and tethering of the anterior leaflet · dilation of the right atrioventricular junction. Increasingly, the trend is for earlier correction of the anomaly, because this has a significant positive impact on overall survival.

stem: A 75-year-old man is assessed on the ward following admission with shortness of breath, progressive angina and anaemia. While he has been an inpatient, an upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy has identified a large gastric ulcer which was injected, and echocardiography has identified severe aortic stenosis. One year earlier, he was still able to walk up to 4 miles a day with his dog. He is now unable to walk upstairs without dizziness and breathlessness. His blood pressure is 138/85 mmHg,and his pulse 75 bpm and regular. He has an ejection systolic murmur. There are bilateral basal crackles on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 97 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) 6.2×10/ 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 302×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 145μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate way to treat his aortic stenosis?
explanation: Aortic Stenosis explanations This patient has severe aortic stenosis and has been relatively well until one year earlier. Surgical valve repair is therefore indicated. The decision between a bioprosthetic valve and a mechanical valve in this case is driven by the need for anticoagulation associated with mechanical valves.In this case, given the gastric ulcer with evidence of significant haemorrhage, anticoagulation is best avoided. This drives the decision towards a bioprosthetic valve, rather than a mechanical one.

stem: A 64-year-old woman presents with chronic left eye pain and visual disturbance, and is diagnosed with open-angle glaucoma, potentially due to impaired drainage of aqueous humour. Where does aqueous humour drain?
explanation: Aqueous humour flows from the ciliary body into the anterior chamber. At the front of the eye, it flows out through the trabecular meshwork and into the canal of Schlemm, and functions as a venous sinus. Blockage of the trabeculae over time can precipitate the development of open-angle glaucoma.

stem: A 48-year-old man is reviewed in the Hepatology Clinic following a third variceal haemorrhage in the past year. He has maintained compliance with carvedilol and eplerenone and refrained from alcohol. Despite this, his symptoms have continued. He was referred for a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt(TIPS) procedure. He asks about potential complications of the procedure. Which of the following is most frequently seen after TIPS?
explanation: HE is the most common complication of TIPS placement. The incidence of HE following TIPS ranges from 30% to 45%,and chronic HE may occur in up to 25% of patients. Risk factors for HE after TIPS include: Q. Answered Flagged ·hyponatraemia · sarcopenia External Links · increased age · prior history of HE Cognitive Impairment Predicts The O... pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26925879/ ·10 mm shunt diameter. Treatment of encephalopathy is as per treatment of the condition before the TIPS procedure taking place.

stem: A 20-year-old student comes to the Emergency Department with an infected human bite on the dorsum of his left hand which he sustained in a ‘play fight'with his flatmate. There is erythema around the marks and it is exuding pus. A wound swab sent by his General Practitioner (GP) has demonstrated Gram-positive cocci. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the positive wound swab?
explanation: S. anginosus is a normal human mouth commensal bacterium found in around 50% of samples from human bites. It is a Gram-positive coccus, which fits with the bacterial growth seen here. The range of mixed bacteria found in a human bite is usually covered by co-amoxiclav, which makes this the appropriate initial intervention in the majority of cases. Quinolones combined with metronidazole can be considered in patients who are penicillin-allergic.

stem: A 28-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with a red, swollen left knee, on which he is unable to weight-bear, and which cannot be flexed more than 30 degrees. He tells you that he fell off his bike a few days earlier and wonders if this is the cause of his knee problem. He has no medical illnesses. You confirm his left knee is hot, swollen and tender. He has some abrasions over the anterior surface. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 144 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 14.3×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 309×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 110 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 171 mg/l 10 mg/L Synovial fluid white cells 50 000/μl 50 000/μl Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Given the fall and the fact this patient is usually fit, the most likely possibility is staphylococcal septic arthritis, with entry of the organisms occurring as a result of the bike accident. Flucloxacillin given IV initially, then orally for up to 4-6 weeks is the intervention of choice. A washout by the Orthopaedic surgeons should also be instigated.

stem: A39-year-old woman comes to the Endocrine Clinic with weight loss, palpitations, anxiety and a persistent tremor which has worsened over the past few months. Her blood pressure(BP) is 110/70 mmHg, and her pulse is 95 bpm and regular. She has a fine tremor at rest and sweaty palms. Her body mass index(BMI) is 20 kg/m. She has a smooth goitre which is mildly tender on palpation. She has bilateral exophthalmos. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 129 g/L 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 238×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 98 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) 0.05 mlU/L 0.5-4.5 mlU/L Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention over the first few months?
explanation: Media explanations Combination therapy with high-dose carbimazole and thyroxine replacement is the intervention of choice. Combination therapy delivered in this way is known as the 'block and replace'approach.This establishes complete suppression of endogenous thyroid hormone production and stable replacement with exogenous thyroxine. By establishing a stable level of thyroxine, this reduces the risk of worsening thyroid eye disease.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) for review, complaining of constipation and aching bones and that she is up passing urine on 2-3 occasions per night. She has hypertension which is treated with ramipril and indapamide, but she is otherwise well. Her blood pressure is 142/90 mmHg, and pulse 72 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 28 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 119 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 259×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 122 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Corrected calcium 2.95 mmol/L 2.1-2.65 mmol/L Phosphate 0.65 mmol/L 0.7-1.5 mmol/L Parathyroid hormone(PTH) 6.7 pmol/l 1.8-6.9 pmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient has symptomatic hypercalcaemia, with a PTH level at the upper end of the normal range and a low serum phosphate level, indicating that primary hyperparathyroidism is the likely cause of her presentation. Hyperparathyroidism Media explanations NICE guidelines are clear on the need for referral: 'Refer people with a confirmed diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism to a surgeon with expertise in parathyroid surgery if they have: symptoms of hypercalcaemia such as thirst, frequent or excessive urination, or constipation or end-organ disease(renal stones, fragility fractures or osteoporosis) or an albumin-adjusted serum calcium level of 2.85 mmol/litre or above.

stem: A75-year-old man is brought by ambulance to the Emergency Department, having been found collapsed on the floor when his home help visited. It is unclear how long he has been on the floor for. He has hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and type ll diabetes. He is unconscious; his temperature is 38.2℃, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg and pulse 95 bpm and regular. He has crackles at the right base on auscultation of the chest. Tone is increased on the right-hand side. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 124 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 16.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 323×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 161 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 5.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 179μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Bicarbonate(HCO-) 19 mmol/L 23-30 mmol/L Glucose 23 mmol/L 11.1 mmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate choice for fluid management? A0.45% saline
explanation: Saline 0.9% is recommended for the management of patients who are likely hypovolaemic(as here). Given the significant elevation in serum Na+and co-morbidities, this patient should ideally be managed on the HDU. Na+should not be corrected faster than 0.5 mmol/Litre/hour (equivalent to 12 mmol/l change in Na+ per day) and should be monitored frequently as fluids are replaced. Monitoring on the HDU with a central line in place helps with monitoring of both the central venous pressure and serum Na+.The elevated sodium here is a pseudohypernatraemia due to relative dehydration (being stuck on the floor). Rather than the sodium being truly high, there is a relative lack of circulating volume(much like in severe DKA).0.9% sodium will, therefore, rehydrate the patient and reduce the sodium slowly.

stem: A 65-year-old man comes to the Cardiology Clinic for review.He has symptoms of shortness of breath and is only able to climb the stairs once per day, despite treatment with ramipril, bisoprolol and furosemide for his cardiac failure. His blood pressure is 122/84 mmHg, and his pulse 64 bpm and regular. He has no ankle swelling and only sparse crackles at both bases on auscultation of his chest. His ejection fraction was measured at 29% some six months earlier. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 135 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 281×109/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 132 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Cardiomegaly,no evidence of Chest X-ray (CXR) left ventricular failure Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention for his cardiac failure?
explanation: In the RALES study, spironolactone used in patients with heart failure and low ejection fraction was associated with a 30% relative reduction in risk of death and a 35% reduction in risk of admission for heart failure. In this patient who is already optimised on other cardiovascular medications, spironolactone is therefore the most appropriate next step. Where patients have significant side-effects from spironolactone, such as breast tenderness, eplerenone is an appropriate alternative.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic for review. She is 16weeks pregnant and is increasingly tired. Her General Practitioner (GP) is concerned that she may have a problem with her thyroid gland. Her blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg,and pulse 75 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 22 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 103 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.4×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 98 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) 0.5 mlU/L 0.5-4.5 mlU/L Total T4 192 nmol/L 58-161 nmol/L Free T4 21 pmol/L 10-23 pmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's raised total T4?
explanation: The increase in oestrogen associated with pregnancy leads to an increase in thyroid-binding globulin. This,in turn, leads to an increase in overall levels of thyroid hormone, although the free fraction of thyroxine actually stays the same. Even though this patient complains of tiredness, it is likely this is a function of normal pregnancy. The patient can be reassured about her condition.

stem: A 42-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic with symptoms of thyrotoxicosis and suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). She has a smooth, mildly tender goitre and exophthalmos consistent with Graves'ophthalmopathy. Which of the following antibodies is the cause of her hyperthyroidism?
explanation: Stimulating anti-TSHR antibodies are responsible for thyrotoxicosis in Graves'disease. They bind to the TSHR and drive increased production of thyroid hormone. Non-stimulating anti-TSHR antibodies are also found in patients with Graves'disease.

stem: A70-year-old man presents to the Haematology Clinic with lethargy, weight loss and night sweats over the past three months. He is particularly concerned, as over the past month, he has begun suffering from headaches and blurred vision and has suffered some bleeding around his gums when he cleans his teeth. He has hypertension but is otherwise well. His blood pressure is 152/90 mmHg,and his pulse 85 bpm and regular.You note a purpuric rash affecting both the upper and lower limbs. His abdomen is soft and non- tender, with no masses. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 124 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) 8.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 271×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 132μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Calcium (Ca) 2.3 mmol/L 2.1-2.65 mmol/L Plasma electrophoresis Immunoglobulin M (IgM) paraprotein band (32 g/L) Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: Waldenstrm's macroglobulinaemia is a B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder which leads to the production of an IgM paraprotein band. This is associated with hyperviscosity which can lead to the formation of microthrombi and is responsible for the headaches and blurred vision that many patients report. In severe cases, it may precipitate an acute stroke. Peripheral neuropathy is seen in up to 50% of patients, potentially associated with anti-myelin-associated glycoprotein activity of the paraprotein. Rituximab-based chemotherapy regimens are the mainstay of therapy, with plasma exchange a potential option in patients presenting with hyperviscosity syndrome.

stem: A 22-year-old student comes to the Emergency Department with an erythematous morbilliform rash which began on her forehead and then spread to involve the neck, trunk and upper limbs over the past 36 hours. She also has lymphadenopathy, conjunctivitis and pharyngitis. She tells you that she has not received the mumps, measles and rubella(MMR)vaccination. Her temperature is 39.3°℃, and pulse 98 bpm and regular. There is quiet wheeze on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 135 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.4×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 187×10/L 150-400×10/ Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 111 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 58 mg/l 10 mg/l Which of the following is the most useful investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation: Measles Media explanations In early measles, detection of measles virus RNA in oral fluid is the investigation of choice. It is detected by reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and remains positive for up to three days after the appearance of the rash. Testing kits can be provided by the Local Health Protection Unit.

stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to the Psychiatry Clinic for review. She is concerned that a need to wash her hands many times a day and avoiding public toilets is impacting significantly on her life. At home, she must wash her hands up to 12 times after each occasion she visits the toilet, and she cannot touch public toilets, such that she completely avoids going out whenever possible so that she can avoid public toilets completely. She feels these problems began after a bout of gastroenteritis some three years earlier. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient's symptoms are consistent with obsessive-compulsive disorder, which has a number of features: Q. Answered Flagged · Either obsessions or compulsions(or both) must be present on most days for a period of at least two weeks. · They originate in the mind of the patient and are not imposed by outside people or influences. · They are repetitive and unpleasant and at least one obsession or compulsion must be present that is acknowledged as excessive or unreasonable. · The subject tries to resist them, although in long-standing OCD,resistance may be minimal. At least one obsession or compulsion must be present which is unsuccessfully resisted. · Carrying out the obsessive thought or compulsive act is not pleasurable. · The obsessions or compulsions cause distress or interfere with the subject's social or individual functioning, usually by wasting time. Obsessive Compulsive Disorder Media explanations Psychological therapies are theinitial intervention of choice.

stem: A 28-year-old woman who has asthma comes to the Emergency Department, having collapsed because of shortness of breath at a local night club. On arrival in the Emergency Department, she is complaining of pins and needles in both hands. Her blood pressure is 105/80 mmHg and pulse 95 bpm and regular, and her respiratory rate is 37 breaths/minute. Investigations: Arterial blood gas Result Normal value pH p(O) 14.2 kPa 10.6 kPa p(CO) 3.2 kPa 4.7-6.0 kPa Bicarbonate 22 mmol/l 23-30 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has acute hyperventilation syndrome, which has led to an acute reduction in p(CO), and a rise in pH.The rise in pH leads to a reduction in ionised calcium, which causes feelings of pre-syncope and pins and needles in the hands. Reassurance and encouragement to moderate her breathing will drive a resolution of symptoms.

stem: 2 1):rv J r1 A 49-year-old man presents to the clinic for review. He has shortness of breath and increasing tiredness, with a persistent thirst over the past four months. His dry cough has not improved despite prescription of a salbutamol inhaler by his General Practitioner (GP). You note an erythematous papular rash on the face, particularly around the nose, and erythema nodosum on both shins. His blood pressure is 145/82 mmHg, and his pulse is 78 bpm and regular. There is no wheeze on auscultation of the chest. His abdomen is soft and non-tender. His body mass index(BMI) is 23 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 136 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) 12.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 302×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 118 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Calcium (Ca+) 2.89 mmol/L 2.1-2.65 mmol/L Bicarbonate (HCO-) 25 mmol/L 23-30 mmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage this patient's hypercalcaemia?
explanation: Corticosteroids are the intervention of choice to treat symptomatic hypercalcaemia in patients with sarcoidosis. There is no indication that the cause of the rise in serum Ca+ is shortterm(eg excess sun exposure), so there is little other option, apart from a course of prednisolone. In the event that corticosteroids cannot be weaned because of symptoms of sarcoid, a steroid-sparing agent such as azathioprine can be instigated. Starting doses of 20-40 mg are usually considered.

stem: A 20-year-old student comes to the ALlergy Clinic for review. He complains that on eating certain foods, he suffers from an itching sensation affecting the inside of his mouth. He has paid for allergy testing from a private General Practitioner(GP), which has revealed an allergy to birch pollen. This is consistent with his symptoms when he gets hay fever in spring. To which of the following foods is he most likely to be allergic?
explanation: This patient has birch apple syndrome, consistent with spring hay fever related to birch pollen. Birch pollen allergy is most associated with food allergy to apples, but allergy is also seen to cherries, plums, apricots and pears. Other reactions are seen to kiwi fruit, carrots and celery. Cooking the food can reduce the risk of food allergy occurring.

stem: A32-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department, complaining of joint pains affecting his right knee, left and right ankles and the toes of his right foot. He also has heel pain affecting his left heel. Of note is that he visited the pharmacy to buy some eye drops for conjunctivitis a few days earlier and had an episode of probable Campylobactergastroenteritis 2-3 weeks ago. You confirm the presence of arthritis affecting both lower limbs and a psoriasis-like rash on the soles of both feet. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 149 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 10.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 302×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 99 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 83 mg/l 10 mg/L Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation: Reactive Arthritis Media explanations This patient has conjunctivitis, oligoarthritis affecting the lower limbs and keratoderma blennorrhagicum,a psoriasis-like rash which affects the soles of both feet. This picture fits with reactive arthritis as a result of his recent episode of gastroenteritis. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents are the usual first step, with a short course of oral steroids in patients who fail to respond. DMARDs can be considered in patients who do not gain adequate symptom relief from corticosteroids.

stem: A32-year-old man comes to the clinic, complaining of excessive daytime sleepiness. His symptoms began after a head injury a few months earlier, sustained after a fall from a horse. He also reports hypnagogic hallucinations, episodes of sleep paralysis, and on a few occasions, at times of stress, he has suffered episodes of collapse and sudden muscular weakness. His blood pressure is 121/81mmHg, and pulse 75 bpm and regular. His body mass index(BMI) is 26 kg/m. His collar size is 16.5. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 142 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count(WCC) 7.4×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 321×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 110 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Calcium(Ca+) 2.1 mmol/l 2.1-2.65 mmol/l Bicarbonate(HCO-) 26 mmol/L 23-30 mmol/L Epworth sleepiness score Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Narcolepsy explanations Narcolepsy is likely, given excessive daytime sleepiness,collapses suggestive of cataplexy and hypnagogic hallucinations with episodes of sleep paralysis. Narcolepsy can be triggered by head injury and can occur post-infection, and increased cases were also reported after vaccination in Scandinavian countries for swine flu. Modafinil is used in patients with narcolepsy to reduce symptoms of daytime sleepiness and may also reduce episodes of cataplexy.

stem: A21-year-old woman presents to the Cancer Genetics Clinic for review. She is very concerned as a number of her first-degree relatives have died from cancer. Identified cancers include breast cancer, leukaemia, soft tissue sarcoma and malignant melanoma. Which of the following is the most likely cause of their familial cancer syndrome?
explanation: Mutations in the TP53 gene, which encodes the P53 tumour suppressor protein, lead to an increased risk of a range of cancers,including breast cancer, soft tissue and osteosarcoma, leukaemia, brain cancers and adrenal cortical tumours. The mutations occur in a familial cancer syndrome (Li-Fraumeni syndrome) where they are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. This is almost certainly the diagnosis here.

stem: You are reviewing guidelines on blood transfusion at the hospital where you work. Over the past few months, there has been increased use of irradiated red cells. Which of the following patients must be given irradiated blood products?
options: A 28-year-old man who has human immunodeficiency virus(HIV) and is taking highly active
A48-year-old woman who has received a renal transplant two years earlier
A 52-year-old man who has non-Hodgkin's lymphoma
A 62-year-old woman who suffered a transient fever after a previous blood transfusion
A72-year-old woman taking fludarabine for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL)
explanation: Fludarabine is a purine analogue, and the class of agents which includes cladribine,fludarabine, deoxycoformycin, clofarabine and bendamustine are associated with a significantly increased risk of transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease. For this reason, patients taking them or who have used them should be prescribed irradiated blood indefinitely.

stem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the Palliative Care Clinic for review. She has metastatic breast cancer with bony metastases and is currently managed with co-codamol 30/500 two tablets four times a day and ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day. You plan to transfer her to oral morphine to further titrate her pain relief, as her pain is not currently adequately controlled. Which of the following daily morphine doses would be appropriate?
explanation: Based on the 100 mg:10mg conversion factor, 30 mg of morphine approximately corresponds to 300mg of codeine. She is currently taking 240mg codeine and has ongoing pain. An increased daily dose, along with as required morphine use, would therefore be indicated.

stem: An 18-year-old man comes to the Renal Clinic for review. He has recently been diagnosed with Alport syndrome. His elder brother also has the condition and has chronic kidney disease(CKD) stage 3b.The patient has a blood pressure of 135/80 mmHg,and his pulse is 70 bpm and regular.His body mass index is 22 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 135 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 291×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine(Cr) 120 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L 24-hour urinary protein 1.8 g 0.15g Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Alport Syndrome explanations ACE inhibitors are the intervention of choice to reduce proteinuria and slow renal progression in patients with Alport syndrome. The condition is caused by a defect in collagen type IV, a major component of the glomerular basement membrane, and is characterised by microscopic haematuria, progressive proteinuria and CKD. It is also associated with deafness. It follows an X-linked inheritance pattern in the majority of cases where men are much more severely affected than women. Angiotensin receptor blockers are an option in patients who fail to tolerate an ACE inhibitor.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is reviewed in the Emergency Department having suffered a syncopal episode after standing still for a prolonged period at a reception. She has no significant medical illnesses and takes no regular medication. Her blood pressure is 118/78 mmHg,and her pulse 67 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's faint?
explanation: Neurally mediated syncope is the most likely diagnosis here,in a young patient with no significant medical illnesses. Vasovagal syncope, the most likely cause here, can have an emotional trigger or be related to orthostatic stress, as here. Other causes of neurally mediated syncope include micturition syncope and syncope precipitated by gastrointestinal stimulation. Carotid sinus hypersensitivity is also classified as neurally mediated syncope and occurs when rotating the head.

stem: You are approached by a drug company who is conducting a trial of a new antiplatelet agent to be combined with aspirin. Which of the following is the mode of action of aspirin?
explanation: Aspirin is a non-selective inhibitor of both COX-1 and COX-2.Low-dose long-term aspirin use blocks the formation of thromboxane A2 in platelets, thereby inhibiting platelet aggregation. It may also reduce leukocyte adhesion and modulate nuclear factor kappa B(NF-kB) signalling, thereby reducing tissue inflammation.

stem: As part of your training portfolio, you are required to complete an audit. Which of the following marks out audit versus clinical research?
options: Time between initial data cut and re-analysis
explanation: Closing the loop, a re-audit against standards is the key principle of a successful audit. Without it, the process is not complete. Where process improvement is put in place, then standards may be progressively tightened with repetitive audit cycles. The timing of the audit cycle depends on the outcomes being assessed.

stem: A 73-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance, having been found on the floor by his home help. He has been unwell for the past few days with a respiratory tract infection, and he apparently fell but was unable to get up. He has multiple co-morbidities, including hypertension and ischaemic heart disease. He is pyrexial with a temperature of 38.8°℃, blood pressure of 105/82 mmHg and pulse of 98 bpm and regular. There are crackles at the left base on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 131 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 15.7×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 303×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 5.6mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 156 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Bicarbonate(HCO-) 18 mmol/L 23-30 mmol/L Creatine kinase(CK) 2436 U/L 22-198 U/L Urine Blood++ on dipstick, no red cells seen on microscopy Chest X-ray (CXR) Consolidation at left base Which of the following is the most appropriate initial way to manage his renal dysfunction?
explanation: This patient has rhabdomyolysis as a result of spending a considerable period of time on the floor. This has resulted in the elevation of CK levels, renal failure with mild acidosis and blood on urine dipstick which is not confirmed on microscopy. Myoglobin is thought to cause renal vasoconstriction, can drive the formation of intratubular casts and is directly toxic to kidney tubular cells. Early treatment is therefore aimed at reducing the accumulation of myoglobin within the kidneys by improving fluid status with intravenous(IV) normal saline replacement.

stem: A 24-year-old man who has moved to the United Kingdom from Russia is referred to the Respiratory Clinic. He has had a chronic cough and night sweats, and has lost 5 kg in weight over the past three months. He smokes 20 cigarettes per day and drinks 10 units of alcohol per week. He has not received the bacille Calmette-Guérin(BCG) vaccination. His blood pressure is 123/82 mmHg, and his pulse is 82 bpm and regular.You note some cervical lymphadenopathy. He has signs of consolidation over the right upper zone on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 120 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 10.2×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 301×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 102 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein(CRP) 82 mg/l 10 mg/l Chest X-ray (CXR) Patchy right upper zone consolidation Mantoux test Positive Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: The presence of weight loss, night sweats, upper lobe consolidation and lymphadenopathy, in the presence of a positive Mantoux test, is consistent with pulmonary tuberculosis until proven otherwise. At least three samples of sputum for microscopy and culture should be sent, and nucleic acid amplification testing should be considered for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The standard anti-tuberculous therapy regimen for pulmonary tuberculosis is isoniazid with pyridoxine, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for two months, then isoniazid with pyridoxine and rifampicin for a further four months.

stem: A 64-year-old man who has diabetes mellitus and hypertension presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset right-sided weakness. The weakness predominantly affects the right side of his face and his right arm, and sensation is diminished on the right-hand side. He has expressive dysphasia and is persistently looking to the left-hand side. Which of the following is the most likely site of arterial occlusion?
explanation: The symptoms seen here fit well with a diagnosis of MCA stroke. MCA occlusions commonly produce the following: Q. Answered Flagged · contralateral hemiparesis · contralateral sensory loss · contralateral hemianopsia · gaze preference towards the side of the lesion · agnosia · receptive or expressive aphasia (dominant hemisphere lesions). Weakness of the face and upper limb is usually more marked than lower limb weakness.

stem: A 44-year-old man comes to the clinic for evaluation of his breathing. He is feeling increasingly tired and according to his wife,he snores every night. He has asthma diagnosed by his General Practitioner, but he is otherwise well. His blood pressure is 148/85 mmHg,and his pulse is 78 bpm and regular. His chest is clear. His abdomen is soft and non-tender, and he is obese with a body mass index of 37 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 140 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 382×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine(Cr) 110 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Bicarbonate (HCO-) 32 mmol/L 23-30 mmol/L Which of the following is the biggest pointer towards obesity hypoventilation syndrome?
explanation: An elevated serum HCO- is consistent with chronic carbon dioxide retention and renal compensation, and is a strong pointer towards underlying obesity hypoventilation syndrome. A serum HCO level of27 mmol/L has a 97% negative predictive value for obesity hypoventilation syndrome and is therefore an ideal initial investigation before moving on to arterial blood gas measurement. An overnight sleep study is the optimal way to confirm the diagnosis, with continuous positive airway pressure(CPAP),coupled with weight loss, as the optimal intervention.

stem: A 68-year-old woman is admitted to the Ophthalmology Ward with an episode of acute angle closure glaucoma. She is prescribed timolol, prednisolone, pilocarpine and phenylephrine eye drops, and acetazolamide tablets. Which of the following is the mode of action of timolol?
explanation: Beta blockers, such as timolol, lead to a reduction in intraocular pressure, primarily by reducing the production of aqueous humour.This is complementary to other interventions, such as use of anticholinergics, in the management of acute glaucoma. In some patients, systemic absorption of timolol via the eye can lead to clinically significant bradycardia.

stem: A 21-year-old student comes to the Emergency Department with swollen, painful testes. He had developed fever and parotitis with severe headache, and was thought to have mumps, according to the General Practitioner(GP) at the Student Health Service. He has never received a vaccination for mumps. His temperature is 38.9°℃, blood pressure 105/80 mmHg and pulse 96 bpm and regular. He has bilateral parotitis and orchitis. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 137 g/lL 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) 8.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 301×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 118 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Bicarbonate(HCO) 25 mmol/L 23-30 mmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 71 mg/l 10 mg/L Anti-mumps immunoglobulin M(lgM) Positive Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for orchitis in this patient?
explanation: Supportive therapy is the intervention of choice for mumps infection. Paracetamol is used as an antipyretic, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs(NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen, used in combination with paracetamol, are particularly effective in combatting pain related to orchitis.

stem: A 64-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with a four day history of a cough and pyrexia. She has hypertension, for which she takes 2.5mg of bendroflumethiazide each day, but is otherwise well. Her temperature is 38.2℃, and her pulse is 89 bpm and regular. Her blood pressure is 159/85mmHg She has crackles at the right base on auscultation of the chest. Her Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 13/15. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 117 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 13.4×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 121 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 120 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for this patient's hyponatraemia?
explanation: This patient has hyponatraemia probably as a result of her lower respiratory tract infection combined with chronic use of bendroflumethiazide.Given her blood pressure is elevated and there is no evidence of renal impairment, fluid restriction is the most appropriate initial intervention.

stem: A74-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer who has extensive bony metastases is reviewed in the Palliative Care Clinic with respect to his pain control. He currently complains of pain in his lumbar spine,both femurs and his right humerus. Currently,his medication includes anti-androgen therapy, morphine 80 mg twice daily, paracetamol 1 g four times daily and ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily. He also takes medications for nausea and constipation. His blood pressure is 145/90 mmHg, and his pulse is 85 bpm and regular. His body mass index is 23 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 98 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 10.9×10/L 4-11×109/L Platelets(PLT) 231×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 132 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Calcium (Ca+) 2.3 mmol/L 2.1-2.65 mmol/l Glucose 8.1 mmol/L 11.1 mmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for control of his bone pain?
explanation: IV ibandronate and IV zoledronate are both potential options to control pain from bony metastases in prostate cancer. A study compared IV ibandronate to radiotherapy and found no difference between outcomes at 4 or 12 weeks. Another agent used in treatment of osteoporosis, denosumab, can also been used for treatment of bony metastases. Vitamin D and calcium supplementation may also be required in patients treated with zoledronate.

stem: A 23-year-old woman who is 16 weeks pregnant comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. She has developed itchy, red, raised nodular lesions on both shins which have become more prominent over the past two weeks. Her pregnancy has been uneventful so far and she has no health issues. Apart from the nodular rash, physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her skin changes?
explanation: The description of the rash here fits with a diagnosis of erythema nodosum. Pregnancy is a well-known cause of this erythematous, nodular rash, as is use of the combined oral contraceptive pill. Other causes of erythema nodosum include tuberculosis, sarcoidosis and Mycoplasma pneumonia. Flares of the skin rash may also be associated with worsening symptoms of inflammatory bowel disease. Most cases are self-limiting, including in pregnancy, and require no specific intervention. Non-steroidal anti- inflammatory drugs(NSAIDs) may be useful for symptom relief outside pregnancy, and potassium iodide or corticosteroids are other potential therapeutic interventions.

stem: A 52-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She has abnormal liver function tests noted by her General Practitioner(GP) and is attending the clinic to discuss management of her condition. She is obese with a body mass index(BMI) of 35 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 115g/lL 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.7×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 143×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/Ll Creatinine (Cr) 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 322 U/L 10-40 U/L Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 188 U/L 20-48 U/L Alkaline phosphatase 167 U/L 50-120 U/L Bilirubin 15μmol/L 2-18 μmol/L Ultrasound liver Fatty infiltration Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for her liver disease?
explanation: This patient is morbidly obese with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease(NAFLD) and possibly NASH. A measure of liver stiffness, such as a fibroscan or magnetic resonance elastography, is important to estimate the degree of liver fibrosis and guide therapy. In the first instance, weight loss of 10% or more is thought to significantly reduce liver fat and liver inflammation and is therefore the preferred intervention. Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) agonists, such as liraglutide, licensed at high dose for treatment of obesity, also have positive data on improving histology in patients with NASH.

stem: A 76-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She complains that over the past few years, she has found it increasingly difficult to hear people talking/conversations in crowded places, and that speech seems muffled or slurred. She has hypertension and has had a previous inferior myocardial infarction, but is otherwise well. Her blood pressure is 139/82 mmHg,and her pulse 70 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hearing loss?
options: Loss of inner ear hair cells
explanation: Loss of inner ear hair cell function is the primary cause of senile hearing loss. The progressive loss of hair cell function leads to gradual hearing loss over a number of years and difficulty with hearing speech, particularly in crowded locations. Specifically,the damage occurs to the stria vascularis, which is responsible for mechanical to electrical signal transduction.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents to the clinic for review. She tells you that she is constantly worried about her appearance and the shape of her body, and has now undergone a range of cosmetic procedures, including breast surgery, lip filler injection and surgery to change the shape of her chin. She is now worried about the shape of her nose and says that it is making her feel so depressed that she wakes at 05:00 every morning thinking about it and is unable to go out for fear of people's opinions about her. Physical examination is entirely normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Q. Answered Flagged As long as patients can commit to it, individual CBT is the intervention of choice for patients with body dysmorphic disorder.CBT in this context is designed to challenge negative appraisal of body image. This includes challenge on how patients see themselves as an aesthetic object, safety behaviours (such as attempts to alter appearance), working to improve the overall mood and ways to break the cycle of excessive rumination on ugliness. This can be complemented with exposure and response prevention therapy(ERP). ERP aims to reduce behaviours such as mirror checking, camouflaging and other compulsive actions. It is also aimed to reduce avoidance of social situations.

stem: A 61-year-old woman who has persistent diarrhoea presents to the Gastroenterology Department for review of her colonoscopy results. She takes a number of medications for diabetes, cardiovascular disease and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Her biopsies reveal microscopic colitis. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her colitis?
explanation: Proton pump inhibitors(PPls), including lansoprazole, are well recognised as a cause of microscopic colitis where biopsy has confirmed the diagnosis and withdrawal followed by re-challenge has precipitated the return of symptoms. When microscopic colitis is confirmed, then withdrawal of the PPI results in a slow resolution of symptoms over weeks or months. A small number of other drugs have also been confirmed as causes of microscopic colitis; these include non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs(NSAIDs), acarbose and ranitidine. A range of other medications are associated with the disease.

stem: A 24-year-old traveller comes to the Emergency Department some four weeks after returning from an extended trip to Thailand. During his trip, he had unprotected sexual intercourse with a number of casual partners. He says that during his trip,he did develop a painless ulcer on his glans penis, which took some time to heal. Examination reveals a number of macular, erythematous lesions measuring up to 2 cm across, affecting predominantly the palm of his hands and the sole of his feet, although some lesions are also appearing on his body. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his skin rash?
explanation: The initial glans penis lesion,followed by the more generalised macular rash, is suspicious of a diagnosis of secondary syphilis. Other features can include uveitis, meningitis, cranial nerve palsies and hepatitis. A single dose of 2.4 MU of penicillin intramuscularly is the intervention of choice. Azithromycin 2 g as a single dose can be given in patients who are penicillin-allergic.

stem: A78-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She has obesity, type ll diabetes and osteoarthritis and complains of urinary incontinence over the past year. She says this is made worse with sneezing, coughing or when she strains to get up out of a chair. Examination reveals a body mass index(BMI) of 33 kg/m,and pelvic examination reveals a urethral prolapse. Urine testing at the General Practice has revealed intermittent blood and proteinuria and positivity to nitrites, which has been treated each time with nitrofurantoin. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her incontinence?
explanation: Stress incontinence is the most likely diagnosis where involuntary leakage of urine on effort or exertion or on sneezing or coughing occurs. This is due to an incompetent bladder sphincter. Stress incontinence may be associated with genitourinary prolapse, as here,and can be worsened by obesity. Weight control and pelvic floor exercises are the initial management of choice. This patient may also benefit from a ring pessary and should be assessed by a uro-gynaecologist.

stem: A 64-year-old man is reviewed on the Stroke ward a few days after suffering a large middle cerebral artery stroke. He is noted to have global aphasia. Which of the following is the most likely location of the lesion causing this patient's aphasia?
explanation: Global aphasia occurs when extensive damage occurs to the left perisylvian region, white matter, basal ganglia and thalamus. Symptoms are marked and generalised deficits in comprehension, repetition, naming and speech production are seen.

stem: A 43-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with one of her work colleagues. She has been taken unwell at a company sales conference where she told the team that she can speak ten languages and would lead the team to victory, having a 100% understanding of the problems ahead. When she arrives at the hospital, she tells you that she is related to the royal family and that she is very important person. She has clear pressure of speech and tells you that she can predict the chances of recovery of other patients in the department. She refuses physical examination. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her confusion?
explanation: This patient's presentation is consistent with a first episode of mania. Obvious features consistent with the diagnosis include delusion of grandeur(related to the royal family, able to speak multiple languages,knows 100% how to deliver for the team), pressure of speech and an over-exuberant choice of clothes. Both olanzapine and risperidone can be used to manage an acute psychotic episode associated with mania.

stem: A 23-year-old woman of Han Chinese ethnic origin comes to the clinic for review. She has recently been diagnosed with complex partial epilepsy. She has no other past medical history. Which of the following is the most appropriate anti-epileptic medication for her?
explanation: Levetiracetam has established efficacy for the treatment of complex partial epilepsy. It also does not carry the same liability with respect to risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome as oxcarbazepine and carbamazepine, making it the default first choice here. Changes in behaviour, including increased aggression, are seen in some patients who take levetiracetam.

stem: A 54-year-old woman with breast cancer comes to the clinic for review. She is currently treated with letrozole. Which of the following best describes the mode of action of letrozole?
explanation: Letrozole is a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor. It inhibits the aromatase enzyme by competitively binding to the haem of the aromatase cytochrome P450, resulting in a reduction of oestrogen biosynthesis in all tissues where aromatase is present. It reduces the production of oestrogen by up to 95% in women who are prescribed it. Side-effects are consistent with a rapid fall in oestrogen levels. B5-alpha reductase inhibitor 5-alpha reductase inhibitors are used in the treatment of benign prostatic hypertrophy. They prevent conversion of androgen substrates to dihydrotestosterone, a more potent androgen which drives prostatic hypertrophy.

stem: A 20-year-old student presents to the Emergency Department with 10 kg weight loss over the past month, as well as polyuria, polydipsia and balanitis. He has no significant medical illnesses. His blood pressure is 105/80 mmHg, with a postural drop of 15 mmHg on standing. His body mass index is 19 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 159 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 9.8×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 301×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.8 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine(Cr) 142 μmol/l 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 28 mmol/L 11.1 mmol/L Which of the following antibodies is most likely to be positive?
explanation: Diabetes -Typel Media explanations Anti-GAD65 antibodies are a useful marker of autoimmune beta-cell attack, particularly in adults presenting with diabetes mellitus.The symptoms here are of insulinopenia,making type I diabetes most likely. ALthough the exact percentage differs across case series, around 60% or more of adults presenting with typel diabetes for the first time are anti-GAD65 positive.

stem: A 67-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with nausea, vomiting and right upper quadrant pain. This is his third attendance at the hospital with similar symptoms over the past six months. He has type ll diabetes, for which he takes metformin, and hypertension which is treated with ramipril. His blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg, and his pulse is 92 bpm and regular. His temperature is 38.2℃. Abdominal examination reveals tenderness in the right upper quadrant. His body mass index is 33 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 145 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 15.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 323×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.6 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 89 U/L 10-40 U/L Aspartate aminotransferase(AST) 78 U/L 20-48 U/L Alkaline phosphatase 195 U/L 50-120 U/L Bilirubin 20 μmol/L 2-18μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: This patient is pyrexial with right upper quadrant pain and an obstructive picture on liver function testing. This fits best with a diagnosis of cholecystitis, and an ultrasound scan of the abdomen to confirm the diagnosis is the most appropriate next step. Many patients can be managed medically with intravenous fluid support, antibiotics and pain relief, with elective cholecystectomy at a later stage.

stem: A71-year-old man is reviewed in the clinic after his third admission in the past year with right lower lobe pneumonia, thought to be related to aspiration. He also complains of a chronic cough, difficulty swallowing and persistent halitosis. He has lost 2 kg in weight over the past year. He smokes five cigarettes per day and uses a salbutamol inhaler. Physical examination is unremarkable. explanation: Pharyngeal pouch explanations The picture here of chronic dysphagia with halitosis and recurrent aspiration pneumonia is typical of that seen in pharyngeal pouch.It is rotting food within the pouch which leads to halitosis, and regurgitation of food material from the pouch which leads to aspiration pneumonia. explanation: This patient's symptoms of back pain, lethargy and night sweats fit well with a haematological malignancy.
